extracted.intended_audience: reviewers for ACL Rolling Review / ACL-area peer reviewers (NLP / computational linguistics)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for performing peer review on the ACL Rolling Review platform: assignment checks, writing reviews, scoring, discussion, ethics, and platform procedures specific to NLP/ACL venues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidentiality of submissions and reviews
rubrics_metrics.description: All the information about submissions and reviews that you receive as part of your assignment is confidential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not discuss individual submissions on social media in ways that allow identification; do not submit confidential information to third-party services (including some generative AI services) that may retain or use that information; confidentiality extends to review reports which may contain confidential information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anonymity and discovering author identity
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers should not actively try to discover the identity of the authors and should not let suspicion or knowledge of author identity affect judgement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Workflow: (1) read the paper and form first impression, (2) search for related work only after forming an impression and avoiding deliberate attempts to find the submission's authors. If you identify or suspect the authors, disclose this in the ARR review form and contact the area chair if reassignment is appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allocate time for reviewing and discussion
rubrics_metrics.description: Block calendar time for checking assignments, working on reviews, and submitting on time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estimate time by measuring your typical skimming and in-depth reading times and time to write ~half a page. Spread work over days to avoid knee-jerk reactions. Also reserve time for reading author responses and participating in discussions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expertise check before accepting assignment
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon assignment, skim the paper to check whether you are qualified to review it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If outside your subfield, it's acceptable if you understand core methodology and common argument styles. If your expertise doesn't cover parts of the submission, state which parts you did not check and indicate your confidence score in the review form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict of interest (COI) and recusal
rubrics_metrics.description: If you know or can guess who the authors are or have other academic COIs, consider recusal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a case may severely compromise your judgment (personal relationships, imminent collaboration, etc.), ask the area chair for reassignment. Recuse if submission is too close to your own forthcoming work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicate unreviewed parts
rubrics_metrics.description: If you are qualified for some aspects but not others, explicitly state what you did not check (e.g., proofs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This helps ACs understand the scope of your review and which parts were not scrutinized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer checklist for possible desk rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: A short checklist reviewers must complete to flag problems that may qualify a paper for desk rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This checklist is quick (usually <30 minutes) and includes appropriateness, hallucinated references, anonymity violations, style/length violations, missing Limitations section, responses to Responsible NLP checklist, ethics issues (may trigger extra ethics review), dual submissions, and extremely similar submissions. Provide justification when flagging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness / scope (desk-reject criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Is this submission appropriate for ARR and the CFP of the relevant conference?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If in doubt, compare to ARR CFP or related conference CFP (e.g., NAACL theme). If obviously out of scope, flag for desk rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hallucinated references or citations (desk-reject criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Check carefully for fabricated or hallucinated references, which threaten scientific reliability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hallucinated references are a serious concern and should be flagged. This check is part of the desk-reject checklist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anonymity violations (desk-reject criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Submissions should be properly anonymized (no explicit references to authors' prior work, identifying acknowledgements, or non-anonymous repository links).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If anonymity appears violated, flag. Note: non-anonymous preprints are permitted for ARR since Jan 2024, but submissions still must be anonymized in the paper itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Style guide or length violations (desk-reject criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Papers that substantially violate venue style guides or exceed page limits should be desk-rejected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Page limits: 4 pages for short, 8 for long (excluding ethical considerations and limitations). Check adherence to specified style guides.

rubrics_metrics.name: Missing Limitations section (desk-reject criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the paper lacks a Limitations section where required, consider desk rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many *CL venues require Limitations; missing this is a red flag at the checklist stage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inappropriate responses to Responsible NLP checklist
rubrics_metrics.description: Egregious or un-justified answers on the Responsible NLP checklist may qualify for desk rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Minor honest mistakes may be excused; at checklist stage ensure authors provide a reasonable indication of where checklist answers are found. Starting Dec 2024, egregious violations can be desk-rejection grounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possible ethics issues (flagging guideline)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ethics issues are not automatic grounds for desk rejection but can be grounds for sending the paper to a dedicated ethics review team.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide justification when flagging; use the dedicated ethics flagging guidelines. Many ethics questions are addressed in the Responsible NLP checklist; if you lack expertise, flag for ethics reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dual submissions and concurrent review policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Submissions to ARR should not be under review elsewhere except in specific exceptions (e.g., notification date overlaps).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ARR checks for dual submissions, but if you spot the same paper in another cycle, notify the AC.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extremely similar submissions and plagiarism concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: If a submission is very similar to another submission or published work, notify AC and consider filing an incident report for publication ethics committee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: File an official comment addressed to AC/SAC/PC and coordinate with chairs for incident reporting as necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read paper at least twice; adjust expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid critiquing on the first read; form an initial impression before searching related work or making criticisms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First skim to identify research question and claims (don’t look at results immediately), then a careful in-depth read to evaluate technical soundness, evidence, proofs, novelty. This avoids hindsight and confirmation biases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Postpone related-work searches until after drafting review
rubrics_metrics.description: Search for related work only after drafting your review to avoid deanonymization and bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliberately searching for the submission's preprint can reveal authors and introduce bias. If you do discover identities, disclose in the review form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appendices: required vs optional reading
rubrics_metrics.description: The paper should be readable by itself; appendices provide extra details but are not required reading unless the main text refers to them for key points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a question pertains to material explicitly deferred to the appendix, look it up. If appendix content should be in the main paper, suggest moving it there (not necessarily a fatal weakness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Be specific in criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Flag issues with sufficient specificity and ideally so that area chairs can understand the problem without reading the entire paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replace vague statements (e.g., 'The paper is missing relevant references') with explicit ones (e.g., 'The paper is missing references XYZ'). Provide line/section pointers, concrete comparisons, or names of missing baselines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid common reviewer heuristics and biases (H1: H17)
rubrics_metrics.description: A list of common problematic heuristics reviewers may use; reviewers should check whether their criticisms are examples of these biases rather than genuine weaknesses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See individual heuristics below (H1–H17). If your weakness corresponds to one of these heuristics, revisit the paper with an open mind and provide evidence/references when asserting prior work or lack of novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: H1: 'The results are not surprising'
rubrics_metrics.description: Finding results unsurprising does not imply they are known or useful to the community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many intuitive findings have not been empirically tested; don't dismiss work only because results seem obvious in hindsight.

rubrics_metrics.name: H2: 'The results contradict what I would expect'
rubrics_metrics.description: A surprising result may reflect confirmation bias on the reviewer's part.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you see a contradiction, ensure your counterargument is evidence-based rather than reflecting prior beliefs.

rubrics_metrics.name: H3: 'The results are not novel'
rubrics_metrics.description: If you think the method/result is previously published, provide references (note policy on concurrent work).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Missing references to prior published work within 3+ months of submission are a problem; preprints less than 3 months prior are treated differently.

rubrics_metrics.name: H4: 'This has no precedent in literature'
rubrics_metrics.description: Novel work can be hard to evaluate and may be unfairly judged; novelty often makes acceptance harder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be open to novel approaches and motivate why novelty should be penalized if you assert it is a weakness.

rubrics_metrics.name: H5: 'Results do not surpass SOTA'
rubrics_metrics.description: SOTA is neither necessary nor sufficient for contribution — other dimensions (efficiency, generalizability, interpretability, fairness) matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If authors don't claim SOTA, lack of SOTA is not sufficient for rejection; evaluate contribution type.

rubrics_metrics.name: H6: 'Negative results are weak'
rubrics_metrics.description: Negative results can be valuable and reduce publication bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a negative result is well-supported, it should be given fair consideration.

rubrics_metrics.name: H7: 'Method is too simple'
rubrics_metrics.description: Simplicity can be an asset; simpler methods that solve the problem can be preferable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticize simplicity only if it fails to address the research question or is inadequate for the claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: H8: 'Paper doesn’t use my preferred methodology'
rubrics_metrics.description: Interdisciplinary field: different valid methodologies exist (models, resources, analyses, surveys, theory).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not penalize work for methodological differences unless they undermine the claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: H9: 'Topic too niche'
rubrics_metrics.description: Niche work can make significant contributions to a narrow subfield and be appropriate for main tracks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge impact in the context of the target community and claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: H10: 'Tested only on non-English (or only English)'
rubrics_metrics.description: Monolingual or language-specific work is valuable; lack of cross-lingual evaluation isn't automatic grounds for rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether claims overreach the evaluated population; consider language-specific contributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: H11: 'Paper has language errors'
rubrics_metrics.description: Writing quality matters, but clarity is more important than journalistic polish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If writing is comprehensible, favor scientific content over stylistic quality; suggest improvements rather than reject solely for language issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: H12: 'Missing reference X'
rubrics_metrics.description: Per ACL policy, omission of highly relevant published work (3+ months prior) is a problem; more recent preprints may be treated as suggestions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite specific missing works when asserting lack of novelty; for resubmissions compare to the original submission deadline.

rubrics_metrics.name: H13: 'Authors could do extra experiment X'
rubrics_metrics.description: Many extra experiments are always possible; only request extra work when it's necessary to validate the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an extra experiment is required for validity, justify why it is essential rather than a 'nice-to-have'.

rubrics_metrics.name: H14: 'Request comparisons to closed models (🆕)'
rubrics_metrics.description: Requesting comparisons to closed-source models is reasonable only if it directly bears on the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Due to test contamination and lack of reproducibility in closed models, such comparisons are often methodologically problematic and should be requested only with justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: H15: 'Authors should have done X instead'
rubrics_metrics.description: Saying you'd have written the paper differently is not a weakness unless authors' choices prevent them from answering their research question.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different valid approaches exist; argue why an alternative is necessary only when it affects claim validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: H16: 'Limitations ≠ weaknesses'
rubrics_metrics.description: Presence of a Limitations section is not itself a weakness; limitations should be assessed for whether they invalidate claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If limitations completely invalidate the work, motivate that position clearly.

rubrics_metrics.name: H17: 'Citation count ≠ validity'
rubrics_metrics.description: Low citation counts do not imply invalidity; judge work on evidence and argument, not popularity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid equating citation metrics with scientific quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check for common problems in NLP papers (overview)
rubrics_metrics.description: A set of common problems in NLP submissions to watch for (methodology, artifact terms, experimental results, general issues).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are codified as M1–M5, T1–T2, R1–R5, G1–G5 below; use them to identify specific weaknesses in submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: M1: LLM-only evaluation without validation
rubrics_metrics.description: If LLMs are used as automated evaluators, assess whether their reliability in that context is sufficiently validated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask for validation of the LLM evaluator or question conclusions drawn solely from LLM-based evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: M2: Reproducibility issues (methodology)
rubrics_metrics.description: Check whether enough experimental details are provided for reproducibility: hyperparameters, selection protocols, code/data availability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers are not required to run the code, but should assess whether reproduction is possible; reproducibility score focuses on ability to re-run the experiment, not replicability of independent reimplementations.

rubrics_metrics.name: M3: Undisclosed data quality issues
rubrics_metrics.description: If resource papers provide datasets, watch for undisclosed problems with the data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You are not required to check datasets exhaustively, but if you notice undisclosed quality issues raise them as serious concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: M4: Unmotivated selection of models/benchmarks
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should clearly motivate why their chosen sample of models/benchmarks is appropriate for their claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you would choose a different sample, that's acceptable — critique only if selected sample is inappropriate for the claimed contribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: M5: Incomplete assumptions or proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: All assumptions should be explicitly stated; formal claims must have complete and correct proofs (which may be in appendices but properly referenced).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If proofs are missing or incomplete, flag as a substantive methodological weakness.

rubrics_metrics.name: T1: Ethics issues with data collection (artifact terms)
rubrics_metrics.description: If human annotation or data collection is involved, check ethics approvals, compensation, and related Responsible NLP checklist answers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ethics issues are handled by ethics reviewers if flagged; provide justification when flagging for ethics review.

rubrics_metrics.name: T2: Unclear license or release terms for artifacts
rubrics_metrics.description: If the paper provides artifacts (datasets/models), authors should state release/license terms and motivations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers should not make legal judgments but should ensure authors are explicit about release terms and licensing.

rubrics_metrics.name: R1: Analysis issues in experimental results
rubrics_metrics.description: Watch for inappropriate statistics, p-hacking, presenting best-of-N runs without transparency, or poorly-tuned baselines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask for better statistical reporting, fair baseline tuning, and transparency in how results were obtained.

rubrics_metrics.name: R2: Inappropriate scope of claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether the evaluated sample/population justifies the generality of the authors' claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If claims overreach the evaluated data or models, mark as an issue and request recalibration of claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: R3: Hypotheses or speculations presented as conclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims must be supported by evidence; conjectures should be labeled as such.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask authors to distinguish speculation from supported findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: R4: Misleading or inappropriate framing, overclaiming
rubrics_metrics.description: Check whether framing leads to overgeneralized or misleading conclusions (e.g., claiming 'understanding' from benchmark results without validation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Request reframing or additional validation if framing is inappropriate for the evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: R5: Missing or inappropriate statistical significance assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: Main experimental results should have appropriate error bars, confidence intervals, statistical tests, or effect size estimates with details on computation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask for appropriate statistical reporting and details about variability assumptions and computation methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: G1: Unclear research question or contribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the knowledge gap and contribution clearly stated in abstract/introduction with assumptions and limitations?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If contributions are unclear, ask authors to clarify scope, assumptions, and limitations in the main text.

rubrics_metrics.name: G2: Reliance on a bad precedent
rubrics_metrics.description: Methodological choices justified by precedent may inherit flaws; call out reliance on unsound prior methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain why a precedent is unsound and discuss alternatives; update review if discussion changes your view.

rubrics_metrics.name: G3: Missing or misrepresented related work
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should fairly represent prior work and not omit highly relevant published contributions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If key work is missing or mischaracterized, provide references and ask for correction or discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: G4: Key terms too vague or undefined
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors must define key terms and constructs used in claims and evaluation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Request precise definitions and references when terms are vague.

rubrics_metrics.name: G5: Misleading or incorrect citations
rubrics_metrics.description: Citations must accurately reflect the cited papers' content; beware of LLM-generated inaccurate summaries used as citations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Point out incorrect attributions and request corrected citations or reading of cited sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide reproducibility assessment (reproducibility score)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess the paper's reproducibility: whether sufficient details/code are available to re-run the experiments and get roughly the same results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reproducibility score is distinct from replicability; reviewers are not required to run experiments but should judge whether reproduction is feasible given provided details. Justify low reproducibility scores in the review text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the three ARR scores properly: soundness, excitement, overall
rubrics_metrics.description: Starting Feb 2025, reviewers provide three scores: soundness, excitement, and overall recommendation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Soundness must be justified by the review text; excitement is subjective and orthogonal to soundness; overall is a composite reflecting soundness, excitement, novelty, and impact. Low soundness needs explicit faults in the review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure review text justifies soundness and reproducibility scores
rubrics_metrics.description: If you give a low Soundness or low Reproducibility score, the review must explain the reasons explicitly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid low scores without textual justification—this indicates an unfaithful review or reliance on bias/heuristics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain professional, neutral, and constructive tone
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviews should be professional, neutral, and ideally kind; avoid sarcasm and dismissive language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remember authors may be early-career or under stress. Write the review you would like to receive; focus on helping authors improve.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge and update review after author response
rubrics_metrics.description: At least acknowledge the authors' response and update your review if clarifications resolve concerns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If unconvinced, explain why in an update. If updating, append an 'Update:' note describing which issues were resolved and how scores changed; do not merely edit the old review without noting changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Participate in reviewer discussion
rubrics_metrics.description: Engage in discussion with authors and other reviewers, particularly after the authors' response.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discuss the most important points first (ACs may not read very long threads). Respond to other reviewers' points and be open to revising your assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware of social influence among reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Other reviewers' opinions may affect your judgment (convergence to mean, deference to senior reviewers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether changes in your view are warranted by evidence or merely social effects; strong disagreements can indicate interesting or unusual work.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to review resubmissions and repeat/substitute/fresh reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: There are special procedures for resubmissions and for assigning substitute or fresh reviewers; follow ARR resubmission guidelines when applicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check the 'How to review resubmissions' section if the paper links to a previous URL; for substitute reviewers or secondary reviewing, follow platform procedures described in ARR documentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generative AI usage policy for reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers must write the content and argument of the review themselves; use of generative tools to create the first draft of reviews or meta-reviews is not permitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasonable uses: paraphrasing to improve clarity for non-native speakers, tools to check proofs. Do NOT upload manuscripts or parts to non-privacy-preserving generative tools. Confidentiality of manuscript and review extends to AI tool inputs. Reviews that appear LLM-generated are discouraged and may lower confidence in peer review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generative AI concerns with author submissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors must disclose use of generative AI; reviewers should be alert to prompt injections or hidden prompts intended to manipulate assistants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you notice prompt injections or manipulative content, report it to chairs; such submissions may be desk-rejected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secondary reviewer policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Secondary reviewers may assist main reviewers, but the main reviewer remains responsible for submitting the review and for sustained engagement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Main reviewer is the point of contact and accountable for quality; there is a 'Secondary reviewer' field in the form (not visible to authors). Secondary reviewers can be credited in reviewer lists and request certificates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emergency Declaration and Delay Notification procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: If you cannot complete an assignment due to emergency, use the Emergency Declaration form; for small delays use the Delay Notification form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these official forms rather than personal emails to ACs; records are visible to chairs and used for analytics. Excessive delays or late reviews can affect eligibility for reviewer recognition.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to contact the area chair (AC)
rubrics_metrics.description: Contact AC via OpenReview Official Comment (select readers to area chairs) or via email (anonymized on OpenReview but can be found via profile links).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'Official Comment' for forum messages directed at ACs; choose 'area chairs' in the Readers field to message only ACs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep Semantic Scholar / profile info updated for better assignments
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure your Semantic Scholar, DBLP, and ACL Anthology profiles are accurate to improve automatic paper-reviewer matching.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delete irrelevant or misattributed papers from your profile, add DBLP/ACL Anthology links; ORCID integration is planned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review report license agreement and data donation
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers can opt in to donate peer review reports to an anonymized public dataset via a license transfer for a cycle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision is made per cycle in your task log; donation transfers all review reports of that cycle in bulk; see ARR blogpost for details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flagging for ethics review (how to decide)
rubrics_metrics.description: If you see potentially serious ethical issues (data collection, potential abuse, disproportionate harms), you may flag the paper for ethics review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide justification when flagging; ethics reviewers will make recommendations about accept/reject/revise on ethical grounds. Use Responsible NLP checklist answers to assess authors' claims about ethics where applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not upload manuscripts or review content into non-privacy-preserving AI tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Uploading submissions or peer review reports to non-privacy-preserving generative tools may violate confidentiality, IP, or data privacy rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid sharing any confidential submission material with third-party services that retain input data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report and document instances of poor or irresponsible reviewing
rubrics_metrics.description: ARR provides mechanisms for authors and chairs to report rude, terse, or otherwise irresponsible reviews; ACs and senior chairs may act on such reports.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors can report common issues with reviews; ACs can use these reports when writing meta-reviews. Egregious irresponsible reviewers may be made ineligible for subsequent cycles per ACL policy (May 2025 onward).

rubrics_metrics.name: Guidance on reviewer incentives and sanctions
rubrics_metrics.description: ACL has policies for recognizing great reviewers and for sanctioning highly irresponsible reviewers or chairs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Great reviewers may be nominated and receive recognition or rewards; highly irresponsible reviewers may be desk-rejected from the cycle and ineligible for future commitments or submissions in the following cycle.

rubrics_metrics.name: How paper assignments are determined
rubrics_metrics.description: Assignments are generated automatically using areas, prior work, languages, reviewer seniority, and institution diversity; ACs check assignments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers should choose accurate areas and keep profiles updated; the system tries to ensure at least one non-student reviewer and no two reviewers from the same institution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy on reviewers reporting author identity discovery
rubrics_metrics.description: If a reviewer uncovers or believes they can identify authors, they should disclose that information in the ARR review form and inform the area chair (not other reviewers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In some cases reassignment is appropriate; disclosure allows ACs to take identity into account when making final decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of specific vs vague review comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Concrete examples for rewriting vague comments into actionable, specific ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples provided: 'The paper is missing relevant references' → 'The paper is missing references XYZ'; 'X is not clear' → 'Y and Z are missing from the description of X.' Use these patterns to make reviews useful to chairs and authors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommendation about reading and using appendices
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should put essential information in the main paper; appendices are for supplementary details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers don't have to read appendices unless the main paper references them for key claims; if appendix material belongs in the main text, suggest moving it.
